input: The Sherwood number is a dimensionless group that plays a central role in the analysis of mass transfer, and it is helpful to develop a clear physical picture of what it represents before it is used in design calculations. In essence, the Sherwood number expresses the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface, bringing together in a single quantity the relative importance of the two mechanisms by which a species can be transported through the fluid adjacent to the surface. When the value is near 1, the implication is that convection contributes little beyond what diffusion alone would achieve, and the transfer process is essentially diffusion-controlled in character. When the value is large, by contrast, convection is the dominant mechanism, the fluid at the surface is continually renewed, and transfer proceeds much more rapidly than diffusion alone would allow. The group is encountered throughout the treatment of gas absorption, liquid extraction, and drying, and in each of these operations it performs the same service of separating the contribution of the flow from the contribution of molecular motion. A sound grasp of these two limiting cases provides the foundation on which the use of the group in correlations and in equipment sizing is built.
target: The Sherwood number compares two routes by which a species crosses the fluid at a surface: transport carried by the moving fluid, and transport by molecular diffusion. The Sherwood number is defined as the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. A value near 1 means the two routes contribute on comparable terms: convection adds little to the transfer that diffusion alone would give, and the rate is set largely by the diffusive step across the fluid at the surface. A large value means convection dominates. The flow continually renews the fluid at the surface, the layer across which diffusion must act is kept thin, and the transfer rate stands well above the rate that diffusion alone would sustain. The number is dimensionless, and it carries neither the size of the equipment nor the identity of the species into the comparison; two arrangements handling different duties can be set side by side on the strength of the number alone. Read in this way, the group tells the engineer which mechanism an improvement must attack: where the value is large, the diffusive step is already short and further gain lies in the surface or the driving force; where the value is near unity, the flow pattern at the surface is the limiting element and is the place to work.
